query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a sliding-induced dynamic grain refinement strategy that promotes amorphization at the tribological interface will create a nano-structured lubricious layer in the CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy, reducing friction and wear consistently from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy with a conventional coarse-grained structure exhibiting higher friction and wear at extreme temperatures.
generation.intervention: Dynamic grain refinement via sliding‐induced amorphization to form an ultra-fine or amorphous self-lubricating surface layer.
generation.conditions: Sliding tests performed across a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C under variable loads in controlled environments.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined, amorphous surface layer with a nano-structured grain size that alters contact mechanics.
generation.mechanism: The intervention is expected to work by generating in situ a nano-structured amorphous layer during sliding, which reduces interfacial shear strength and provides self-lubricating properties, thereby lowering friction and wear across the temperature range.
generation.predicted_outcome: The intervention will produce a lower and more stable coefficient of friction and reduced wear rate relative to the unmodified CoCrFeNi alloy, sustained over the full temperature range and under varied loads.
generation.baseline: Baseline performance is defined by the unmodified CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy, which typically shows increased friction and wear at both low and high temperature extremes.
generation.boundary: Effective within the temperature range of room temperature to 800 °C, under the tested load conditions and in controlled environmental conditions; performance may vary outside these specified boundaries.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of friction reduction and wear improvement is uncertain and may depend on the precise kinetics of in situ amorphization and the micromechanical interactions at the sliding interface under varying conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct sliding wear tests comparing CoCrFeNi specimens with and without pre-induced conditions favoring dynamic grain refinement. Tests should span temperatures from room temperature to 800 °C, with variable loads under controlled environmental conditions.
measurements: Coefficient of friction measured continuously during sliding
Wear rate assessed via mass loss and surface profilometry
Microstructural characterization (e.g., TEM, XRD) to confirm the formation of an amorphous, refined grain layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If specimens treated to promote dynamic grain refinement do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in friction and wear over the full temperature range compared to controls, or if microstructural analyses do not reveal the presence of the expected amorphous/nano-structured layer, the hypothesis will be falsified.

chosen.approach: Dynamic grain refinement via sliding‐induced amorphization
